units.name: public-api
units.role: The front door users import and call to make HTTP requests, and to reach every other public name the library offers.
units.description: This is the very first thing a program touches when it says `import requests`. It offers a handful of simple functions — get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options, request — that a caller uses to fetch or send data over the web without needing to know anything about connections, cookies, or sessions. Under the hood it does no networking itself: for every call it quietly creates a short-lived conversation with the server (a Session), hands the real work off to it, and closes it when done. It also does a little housekeeping when the library first loads, such as warning the user if the versions of its supporting libraries look too old to work correctly.

False positive from a mechanical text scan: api.py and __init__.py each contain '>>> import requests' inside a docstring usage example. Neither file makes a direct network call; both delegate to the session unit, which delegates in turn to the transport-adapter unit.

units.name: session
units.role: Owns the Session object that conducts a stateful sequence of HTTP requests: merges defaults with per-request options, dispatches through a transport adapter, follows redirects, and persists cookies across calls.
units.description: This is the 'conversation' object of the library. When a program wants to make several web requests that should share things like login cookies, custom headers, or proxy settings, it creates a Session. The Session remembers those shared settings, combines them with whatever is different about each individual request, hands the actual work of talking to the network off to a lower-level connector, and keeps track of anything the server sends back — like cookies — so later requests in the same session behave consistently. It must never send a request without first combining session-level and per-call settings correctly, and it must stop following redirects once a sane limit is reached.

units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Defines what an HTTP request and an HTTP response are, and turns caller intent into wire-ready bytes and raw server bytes into something a caller can query.
units.description: This part of the library defines the shape of a request and a response, as separate ideas from how they travel over the network. A caller describes what they want — a URL, some headers, form data, files, JSON — using a Request object; that becomes a PreparedRequest, the exact set of bytes and headers ready to be sent. On the way back, a Response wraps whatever the server sent and gives the caller convenient ways to ask questions of it: the status code, the headers, the raw content, the decoded text, the parsed JSON, or a stream of chunks for large downloads. It must never silently swallow a malformed response; it raises a clear error instead.

units.name: auth
units.role: Encodes how to prove identity to an HTTP server via Basic, Proxy, and Digest authentication schemes.
units.description: This part of the code knows the rules for the different ways a program can prove who it is to a website before the server hands over data. It knows how to build the simple 'Basic' authentication header by encoding a username and password, and it knows the more elaborate 'Digest' handshake, where the server issues a challenge and the client must compute a cryptographic proof combining that challenge with the credentials and the request details. It never opens a network connection itself; it only prepares the proof and reacts to a server's '401 Unauthorized' challenge by handing back a corrected request.

entrypoints.name: HTTPBasicAuth

effects.description: HTTPDigestAuth.build_digest_header calls os.urandom(8) as part of the input hashed to produce the client nonce (cnonce).
HTTPDigestAuth.build_digest_header calls time.ctime() and mixes the current time into the cnonce-generation hash.

units.name: transport-adapter
units.role: Opens the actual network connection to a server, verifies TLS certificates, and turns the raw urllib3 response into this library's Response object.
units.description: This is the part of the library that does the real work of talking to a website over the network. Once the rest of the library has assembled a request, this piece hands it to the underlying networking engine, which opens a connection, negotiates HTTPS security by checking the site's certificate against a trusted list, optionally routes through a proxy, sends the request, and waits for a reply. It then repackages that low-level reply into the Response object the rest of the library expects. It must never skip certificate verification unless explicitly told to.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter

units.name: cookie-jar
units.role: Bridges requests' dict-like cookie interface to Python's stdlib http.cookiejar machinery.
units.description: This part of the code is the bookkeeper for cookies — the small pieces of data websites ask a client to remember, like login sessions. It takes cookies that come back from a website and stores them so they can be handled like a normal dictionary, and when a new request goes out it figures out which stored cookies should be attached and formats them correctly. It relies on Python's built-in cookie machinery for the tricky policy work of which cookie belongs to which site and path, and just adapts that to the simpler style the rest of the library wants. It does not save cookies to disk itself.

units.name: http-utils
units.role: Provides HTTP-protocol helper functions — proxy resolution, netrc auth lookup, header/URL parsing, encoding detection, body-size helpers — consumed by the request-building and transport layers.
units.description: This is the toolbox of small, reusable helper functions the rest of the library leans on to talk HTTP correctly. It figures out which proxy server should be used for a given address by reading system settings and environment variables, looks up saved login credentials from a user's netrc file on disk, works out the size of data being uploaded, parses and re-quotes URLs and headers so they are safe to send, and guesses the text encoding of a server's response. It never decides what a request or response means; it must always leave URLs and headers well-formed for whatever calls it next.

units.name: runtime-support
units.role: Generic, domain-agnostic scaffolding — compatibility shims, base data structures, hook dispatch, typing helpers, version metadata — that every other unit imports.
units.description: This group of files does not know anything about HTTP requests, headers, cookies, or sessions. It provides small generic building blocks the rest of the library leans on: smoothing over differences between Python versions and optional third-party packages, two general-purpose dictionary-like containers (one of them used to store headers case-insensitively), a tiny mechanism for running user-supplied callback functions at certain points, an old import path kept alive for backward compatibility, the library's version metadata, and internal type-checking helpers that exist only to help developer tools catch mistakes. It never encodes any rule about what an HTTP request or response is; it only exists to support the units that do.

units.name: exceptions-status
units.role: Defines the shared vocabulary of error conditions and HTTP status codes used throughout requests.
units.description: This unit is the library's dictionary of things that can go wrong, and its friendly names for the standard replies a web server can give. It performs no actions itself — it just gives every other part of the library a common, precise language: a name for 'the connection failed', a name for 'the server took too long', a name for 'that is not a valid web address', plus a way to say codes.ok instead of remembering that 200 means success. Every unit that talks to the network, builds a request, or reads a response relies on these shared names to describe outcomes consistently.

units.name: diagnostics
units.role: Collects Python/OS/library/SSL version information into a bug-report payload, usable as a library function or a CLI command.
units.description: This is a small diagnostic helper that does none of the actual work of sending requests. When a user is filing a bug report, it gathers useful facts about their computer and software setup — the Python version, the operating system, and the version numbers of requests and its supporting libraries — and packages them into a tidy block of text that can be pasted into a bug report, either by calling a function or by running it on the command line.

main() writes the JSON-formatted report to stdout via print()/json.dumps() when run as `python -m requests.help`.

violations_observed.note: utils.py computes DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH by calling certs.where() directly, reaching past the transport-adapter unit's declared HTTPAdapter-centric surface into its certs.py helper. Recorded because the resulting constant then flows back into transport-adapter (adapters.py imports DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH from utils.py), creating a two-hop, cross-unit round trip for one piece of configuration rather than a clean one-directional dependency. Not fixed, since both edges now have listed entrypoints (certs.where and DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH).
